business.title: Krypton-sputtered tantalum films for scalable high-performance quantum devices
business.description: Superconducting qubits and microwave resonators based on tantalum thin films have recently demonstrated large increases in performance. This makes Ta an attractive material for superconducting quantum computing applications, but so far direct deposition has largely relied on high substrate temperatures exceeding 400 °C to achieve the cubic (bcc) phase of tantalum. Here we show that changing the sputter gas from argon to krypton promotes synthesis of bcc tantalum films on silicon at temperatures as low as 200 °C. This provides a wide process window compatible with back-end-of-line fabrication standards. The microwave performance of coplanar-waveguide resonators fabricated from krypton-sputtered films shows an excellent tight performance distribution. Higher-temperature-grown films exhibit higher losses, in correlation with the degree of tantalum–silicon intermixing. Finally, we demonstrate with these films transmon qubits with a compact, 20-μm capacitor gap, achieving quality factors up to 16.9 million. Krypton sputtering is found to promote the synthesis of body-centred-cubic tantalum films on silicon at temperatures as low as 200 °C, compatible with back-end-of-line fabrication standards. Superconducting qubits based on these thin films exhibit excellent performance.

science.title: Telomere to telomere genome assembly of a wild soybean Glycine soja accession HAAS216
science.description: Wild soybean (Glycine soja), the progenitor of cultivated soybean (Glycine max), represents an important reservoir of genetic diversity crucial for soybean improvement. However, the limited availability of high-quality reference genomes for wild soybean has constrained its comprehensive genomic characterization. Here, we present a telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genome assembly of a wild soybean (G. soja) accession HAAS216 with a size of 1,018.17 Mb, generated using PacBio HiFi, ultra-long Oxford Nanopore sequencing, and Hi-C data. The assembly spans all 20 chromosomes and captures 20 centromeric and 40 telomeric regions, forming a gap-free T2T genome assembly. This assembly exhibits superior quality regarding completeness (BUSCO: 99.6%), contiguity (contig N50: 51 Mb), and base-level accuracy (QV: 55.53). Repetitive sequences make up 55.84% (568.57 Mb) of the genome, and 48,390 protein-coding genes were predicted, of which 47,567 (98.30%) were functionally annotated. This genome assembly provides a genomic resource for comparative genomics and facilitates genetic research and crop improvement in soybean.

science.title: OXCT1 knockout suppresses HeLa cell proliferation and invasiveness through adhesion proteins and the PI3K/Akt-Snail pathway
science.description: While the OXCT1 gene (3-oxoacid CoA-transferase 1, and its gene product SCOT; succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase) is primarily recognised as the rate-limiting enzyme in ketone body catabolism, accumulating evidence indicates that ketone bodies and ketogenic diets exert complex, context-dependent effects on cancer progression. In this study, we investigated the functional role of OXCT1 in a cervical cancer model using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene knockout in HeLa cells. Loss of OXCT1 markedly impaired cell migration and invasion while enhancing intercellular adhesion. These changes were accompanied by downregulation of the β-hydroxybutyrate transporter MCT1, increased expression of adhesion molecules such as E-cadherin, and reduced activation of oncogenic signalling pathways including PI3K/Akt and ERK1/2. Furthermore, OXCT1-deficient cells exhibited lower levels of epithelial-mesenchymal-transition (EMT)-associated factors, including Snail, together with reduced clonogenic survival under ketogenic conditions. Collectively, these findings indicate that OXCT1 supports HeLa cells, a cervical cancer cell line, proliferation and invasive potential by promoting metabolic flexibility, adhesion remodelling, and pro-invasive signalling. Our data identify OXCT1 as a potential molecular driver of cervical cancer aggressiveness and a putative target for therapeutic intervention.

science.title: Effects of floating and emergent macrophytes on sediment deposition in Ketar River, Ethiopia
science.description: Ethiopian water bodies severe threatens by sedimentation. However, research on using aquatic macrophytes for biological management remains scarce. This study investigated the effectiveness of Pistia stratiotes and Ludwigia stolonifera in trapping sediment and mitigating re-suspension in the Ketar River during the 2018 rainy season. Results from two months of sediment trap collections showed significant differences between vegetated and open water areas. Sedimentation rates were notably higher in macrophyte stands; the mixed Pistia stratiotes + Ludwigia stolonifera stand achieved the highest rate (34.2 ± 4.44 g DW m-2 d-1), compared to the sole Pistia stratiotes stand (20.6 ± 7.6) and open water (11.72 ± 1.03). Both macrophyte treatments significantly reduced sediment re-suspension, with the mixed stand proving most effective at restraining sediment movement. While water depth and turbidity had no significant effect across sites, the presence of vegetation consistently lowered suspended solid concentrations. These findings highlight the crucial role of macrophytes in reducing re-suspension, indicating that mixed macrophyte communities offer stable and nature-based sediment management solutions. Therefore, the results from this study may be applicable to others threatened Ethiopian water bodies. While the study’s two-month results on two dominant macrophyte species are significant, long-term research is essential to account for seasonal and water-level fluctuations.
